title: A Relationship Between Nonphysical Quasi-probabilities and Nonlocality Objectivity

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: For p = i⊗I the text claims β^Tβ = diag(β_ix², β_iy², β_iz²). However, for this case β (restricted to the relevant G2 points) has only one nonzero ROW (e.g. for p = X⊗I the nonzero entries are β_XX, β_XY, β_XZ in row X). Computing β^Tβ for a matrix with a single nonzero row w=(β_ix,β_iy,β_iz) gives the outer product ww^T, which is rank-1 with entries (β^Tβ)_{kl}=w_k w_l (off-diagonal terms like β_ix·β_iy are generally nonzero), and its eigenvalues are (|w|²,0,0), NOT the three independent values (β_ix²,β_iy²,β_iz²) claimed. The correct eigenvalues are identical in form to the p=I⊗i case (sum,0,0). This directly contradicts the stated formula and is verifiable by explicit matrix multiplication.

predicted_errors.error_location: Equation (9) and surrounding discussion ('This asymmetry in β^Tβ furnishes a swap-intolerant nonlocality...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Because β has rank ≤1 in both the p=i⊗I and p=I⊗i cases (only one row or one column populated), β^Tβ has eigenvalues (S,0,0) in BOTH cases, where S=β1²+β2²+β3². Hence M = sum of two largest eigenvalues = S for both labelings — there is no asymmetry between left- and right-identity placements. The claim that 'These conditions give M > 1 for p = I⊗i (left-identity) but not p = i⊗I (right-identity)' is therefore mathematically unsupported and follows from the erroneous Eq. (8); the conditions in Eq. (9) (e.g. β1²+β2² ≤ 1 for the 'local' labeling) do not actually correspond to M≤1 for that labeling once β^Tβ is computed correctly.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proposition 2.1 and the proof of Theorem 1.4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: From Eq. (7), λ = 1+τ_p ± sqrt(Σ(β_i+τ_i)²) = 1+τ_p ± |E+C| = 1+τ_p ± distance(-E,C), and λ = 1-τ_p ± sqrt(Σ(β_i-τ_i)²) = 1-τ_p ± distance(E,C). Positivity of the minus-branches requires distance(E,C) ≤ r- = 1-τ_p (i.e. E ∈ sphere(C,r-)) and distance(-E,C) ≤ r+ = 1+τ_p (i.e. -E ∈ sphere(C,r+)). This is the opposite pairing from what Proposition 2.1 states ('the state point E and its reflected point −E are contained ... in the spheres (C, r+), (C, r−) respectively'), and the proof of Theorem 1.4 ('the point −E lies on the sphere (C, r₋)... E a distance of |λ₀| from the sphere (C, r₊)') follows this same (incorrect relative to Eq. 7) pairing.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, paragraph discussing Proposition 2.1 ('under translations and rotations of the parameter space S...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims that 'under translations and rotations of the parameter space S, any eigenvalue-dependent property such as positive-definiteness is unchanged.' However, the eigenvalues depend on |E+C| (not just |E−C|). While |E−C| is invariant under any translation, |E+C| is not: translating both E and C by a vector v changes E+C to E+C+2v, which generally changes |E+C|. Only rotations about the fixed origin preserve both |E−C| and |E+C| simultaneously. Thus the stated invariance under 'translations' is mathematically false, even though the paper's actual construction only uses rotations.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, 'It was first described by Bell in 1964 [1], with an experimentally testable inequality discovered in 1966 [2].'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The widely recognized experimentally testable Bell-type inequality is the CHSH inequality, published in 1969 (Clauser, Horne, Shimony, Holt). There is no well-known 1966 publication establishing an experimentally testable Bell inequality; Bell's 1966 paper (Rev. Mod. Phys. 38, 447) addresses hidden-variable no-go theorems, not an experimentally testable inequality. The date/attribution appears to be incorrect.
